title: Herod's Violence, Peter's Rescue, and a King's Fall
summary: King Herod has James the brother of John executed and imprisons Peter during Passover, intending to put him on trial. While the church prays, an angel leads Peter out of prison, and he goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where the believers at first refuse to believe the servant girl who hears him at the gate. Later, at Caesarea, Herod accepts the crowd's praise as a god and is struck down, while the word of God keeps spreading.
story: For the last two chapters the story has moved outward to Caesarea and Antioch. Now Luke turns back to Jerusalem for the last major scene of Peter's ministry in the book. The church that began in Jerusalem faces its first persecution by a Jewish king rather than by the temple leadership, and it loses its first apostle. After this chapter Peter steps aside (he appears again only at the council in chapter 15), James the Lord's brother emerges as a leader in Jerusalem, and the spotlight moves to Barnabas and Saul, who return to Antioch with John Mark. The chapter works as a hinge: the Jerusalem period closes and the mission to the nations is about to begin.
historical:
The Herod of this chapter is Herod Agrippa I, a grandson of Herod the Great. He was raised largely in Rome and was a friend of the imperial family. The emperor Caligula gave him territories in the north, and in AD 41 Claudius added Judea and Samaria, so that for about three years he ruled a kingdom nearly as large as his grandfather's. It was the only time between AD 6 and the Jewish revolt that Judea had its own king rather than a Roman governor. He cultivated the favor of his Jewish subjects, which explains Luke's note that the execution of James pleased the Jewish leadership.

Josephus gives a parallel account of Agrippa's death in AD 44. He describes the king appearing at a festival in Caesarea in honor of the emperor, wearing a robe woven of silver that shone in the morning sun, while flatterers hailed him as a god. Agrippa did not rebuke them, was seized with severe pain in his abdomen, and died a few days later. The two accounts differ in detail but agree on the place, the occasion, the acclamation, and the sudden illness. Because Agrippa's death can be dated, this chapter is one of the few fixed points in the chronology of Acts, and the execution of James falls shortly before it.
cultural:
Peter is arrested during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the week that followed Passover, when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. Herod waits until after the festival to bring him out for a public trial. Four squads of four soldiers each would take turns through the four watches of the night, with Peter chained to two of them and two more at the entrance, a heavy guard that underlines both Herod's intent and the impossibility of escape. Roman practice held guards responsible for their prisoners, which is why Herod has them executed.

Mary's house has an outer gate and a servant, and it can hold many people, which suggests a household of some means. Houses like this were the meeting places of the early church, which had no buildings of its own. Her son John Mark is traditionally linked with the Gospel of Mark. When the believers say, It must be his angel, they reflect a belief found in Jewish thought of the time that individuals had guardian angels who might resemble them (compare Matthew 18:10). Tyre and Sidon, the old Phoenician ports, depended on grain from the Galilean hinterland, as they had since the days of Solomon and Hiram (1 Kings 5:9-11), which gave Herod a strong hand over them.
literary: Luke frames the chapter with contrasts. It opens with Herod reaching out to harm the church and closes with Herod struck down, while the word of God continued to spread and multiply (verse 24). The rescue story is told with vivid detail and gentle humor: Peter must be struck on the side to wake him, dressed step by step like a child, and led past the guards before he realizes he is not dreaming; Rhoda is so overjoyed that she leaves him standing at the gate; and the praying church tells her she is out of her mind. The echoes of the exodus are deliberate. It is Passover, a prisoner is led out by the angel of the Lord at night, and Peter says the Lord has rescued him from Herod's grasp, language that recalls Israel's rescue from Pharaoh.

outline.t: James is killed and Peter imprisoned
An angel leads Peter out of prison
Herod accepts worship and is struck down
The word spreads; Barnabas and Saul return

doctrines.note: The church was fervently praying to God for him (verse 5), and God answered, though the people praying were astonished when he did. The chapter is honest that faithful prayer and surprised unbelief can live in the same room.

Herod has soldiers, chains, and the power of the sword, yet the chapter ends with the king dead and the word of God growing. God's rule over history does not prevent the death of James, but it sets a limit on the power of those who oppose his people.

Herod dies because he did not give glory to God when the crowd called him a god. Ancient rulers were often honored with divine titles; the chapter treats accepting such honor as a fatal offense against the one true God.

words.note: Ektenos, fervently or earnestly, from a root meaning to stretch out. Luke uses a related word for Jesus praying in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). The church's prayer is not casual; it is sustained and strained toward God.

Angelos, messenger or angel. The word appears seven times in the chapter: an angel of the Lord frees Peter, the believers think it must be Peter's angel, and an angel of the Lord strikes Herod. The same messenger of God rescues one man and judges another.

Doxa, glory, the weight and honor that belong to someone. Herod's sin is that he did not give glory to God, taking for himself what belongs to God alone. In Scripture, glory is what God will not share with idols (Isaiah 42:8).

christ: Peter's rescue at Passover repeats the pattern of the exodus, and through that the pattern of Jesus's own death and resurrection, which also took place at Passover. Jesus was arrested at the festival and held by soldiers, and he too came out of a guarded place that should have held him. The difference is instructive: Jesus's deliverance came through death, not around it, which is why James's death is not a defeat. The chapter also sets two kings side by side. Herod dresses in royal robes, accepts worship, and dies. Jesus, the true King, refused to grasp at glory and was exalted by God. The word of God that keeps growing after Herod's death is the word about him.

hard.q: Why did God rescue Peter but allow James to be killed?
hard.a:
Luke gives James's death a single verse and offers no explanation, and the silence is part of the honesty of the chapter. The church presumably prayed for James too. Interpreters have not claimed to know why one apostle died and the other was spared, and the text does not invite speculation about James's worthiness or the church's faith.

What the wider New Testament offers is a way of holding the two together. Jesus had told James and John that they would drink the cup he drank (Mark 10:39), and James did. Peter was also told he would one day die for Christ (John 21:18-19), and church tradition holds that he was later executed in Rome. Rescue in this chapter is a reprieve, not a guarantee. Acts presents both outcomes as within God's rule: God can open prison doors, and he can also receive his servants through death, and neither outcome stops the word of God from spreading.

questions: The believers were praying for Peter's release but did not believe it when it happened. Where might you be praying for something you do not quite expect God to do?
Luke records James's death in one sentence and Peter's rescue at length. How do you hold together God's deliverance of some and the suffering of others?
Herod accepted praise that belonged to God. What forms does that temptation take for people with influence today, including in the church?
